cues.t: [applause]
(Larry Hastings) Thank you. Yes, this talk has changed.
If you're looking for my talk about the GIL, this isn't it.
This is a talk about removing Python's GIL.
And thank you all for practicing getting your planes for later tonight.
So, as a preface for this talk, I want to warn you: this talk is going to be exceedingly technical.
I was encouraged to make this talk very technical, actually, by the program committee.
So I'm going to talk about a lot of technical topics and I don't really have that much time to introduce them.
So, I'm assuming that you're pretty familiar or comfortable at least with me talking about multithreading
and about CPython internals from a very high level.
I'm not going to be digging way down, but you have to understand kind of the basics of CPython internals, like reference counting.
If you're not familiar with that stuff, a good refresher course or an introduction would be my previous talk,
called "Python's Infamous GIL", which, again, I was supposed to give here, but then we switched it.
There's videos of that online. So let's start with a little history about the GIL. The GIL was added in 1992.
Guido wanted to add support for this new thing that operating systems are starting to do, called threading.
And he needed a way of protecting the global and static variables inside of CPython so that you couldn't have races between multiple threads.
And so he added this thing called the GIL 24 years ago.
Let's make no mistake, this was a lovely design and it has served us very well that has a lot of wonderful positive attributes.
I'm not in the camp of GIL haters. I think that that's -- I think people who are GIL haters are kind of misinformed.
So let's talk about the ramifications of this design.
First of all, the GIL was incredibly simple, which meant it was easy to get right, both for us and it was easy
for CPython -- C extension authors to get right.
It had no deadlocks because there's only one lock.
So you can't have deadlocks between two locks because there aren't two locks.
It had very little overhead. You touch the GIL infrequently.
And if you had single-threaded code, it ran incredibly fast because, again, we didn't have
any synchronization overhead, we didn't have any locking and unlocking.
Your code just ran, almost no overhead, and it ensured that -- it sort of paved the way for your code to run very, very quickly.
If you -- if your program is I/O bound and you use multiple threads, then everything worked great,
and this is actually the original use case of threading because computers didn't develop multiple cores until very recently --
or at least, you know, consumer-level hardware.
The problem is, of course, if you run multiple threads and your program is CPU bound, you're kind of out of luck.
The GIL ensures that your code is only going to run on a single core at a time, which was fine in 1992.
It was rare that you would see a multi-core computer back then.
But the world has changed around us over the subsequent 24 years.
So these days, our wonderfully thin and light laptops and our phones and our watches
and our eyeglasses have all gone multi-core.
We live in a deeply multi-core world and Python is still doing single core.
I have a workstation at home that has 28 cores in it.
Like, I want multi-core stuff. But Python just isn't ready for it.
This is a comment actually, sitting in the Python source code right now.
My suggestion is that it's time to consider moving beyond rudimentary thread support.
After all, your computer has all these wonderful resources and Python is able to take advantage of all of them...
...except for the multiple cores.
And this is kind of a sore point. A lot of people, yeah, if you have a problem, you can go multi-process, and of course, yes,
you can take advantage of multiple cores, but there are definitely problem domains where that's not true.
And those people would maybe love to use Python and they just kind of can't.
Now there was an attempt to remove the GIL before.
And when I say "attempt," what I mean is, they successfully removed the GIL.
This was back in Python 1.4 days in 1999.
It was literally, like, December of 1999 the patch was posted.
So, right before the Y2K bug and everyone was nervous.
This change did not require changing the CAPI, so your code usually would still just run.
It took all of those global variables that were in the Python core that Guido was protecting with the GIL and moved them into a single struct
called PyThreadState, which we actually -- that that got merged. We have that today.
It added a single mutex lock around incr and decr.
On Windows it used something smarter called interlocked increment.
And it made your code between four and seven times slower.
So again, I want to just make this point: the GIL makes your code run fast, and removing the GIL makes your code run more slowly,
and that's the challenge of removing the GIL.
So if you want to know more about this free-threading patch, David Beazley wrote a wonderful blog post
called "An Inside Look at the GIL Removal Patch of Lore." Very easy to find on the internet.
I've referred to it a lot. But even that is 15 years ago.
I feel like it's time to try again, so I have this project I'm calling the Gilectomy. That's the surgical removal of the GIL.
And I've thought about the problem a lot.
So, I would say that there are four technical considerations you must take into account when you try to remove the GIL.
Those are: reference counting, of course.
Python objects are reference counted in order to keep track of their lifetimes. Very quickly:
every Python object has a number associated with it called the reference count. If that object is stored in three places --
like, it's a member of a module, and it's stored in a list, and something else -- it'll have a reference count of 3.
Every time you drop your reference, like if you say -- if you remove it from the list, then you decrement the reference count,
so it would have a reference count of 2.
When the reference count reaches 0, you free the object because no one's interested in it anymore.
So that's when you DEL and that's when you reclaim the memory.
Python objects use this, and if you have multiple threads that are both trying to access the object at the same time,
you could have a race between them trying to update the reference count.
You could result in an incorrect reference count and then you're freeing memory too early or freeing it too late and it's a memory leak.
We need to address reference counting in order to run Python on multiple cores simultaneously.
Globals and static variables: there are a fair number of them.
Like, specifically there's a bunch of per-thread information that we would need to ensure was kept separate --
the different threads were kept separate from each other.
And there are a bunch of shared singleton objects like a string, or a module, or the small integers.
Python pre-creates all the small integers and shares those.
And those would of course need to work across multiple threads.
C extensions run in a world right now -- the GIL guarantees that a C extension will only ever run one thread at a time,
unless they explicitly say, "You know what?
"Threads are okay right now." A C extension has never lived in a world where more than one thread
can be running inside it at a time, and they make assumptions about this all the time.
And allowing multiple threads to run inside of a C extension is going to break it, so we needed to address that.
And finally, the atomicity of operations.
If you have a Python dict and you add to it or if you have a Python list and you append to it,
there are a bunch of steps that have to happen in order for that to occur.
And in Python right now, we just guarantee that no other thread can interrupt you while you're doing those operations.
But if we have multiple threads, and a second thread tried to examine that object when you were in one of these incomplete states
where you hadn't finished the append to the list, say, it could see the object in an incomplete state.
So we need to guarantee that objects don't examine -- other threads don't examine objects while they're in these incomplete states.
We need to guarantee that those operations are atomic from the perspective of a Python program.
But in addition to these four technical considerations, I say that there are three political considerations.
Political, kind of a bad word, but it was the best I could come up with.
These are not technical considerations, but these are considerations that are imposed on us by the community
or by things that aren't necessarily a technical thing.
So the first one, Guido has said -- he wrote a blog post in 2007 I'll talk about later, where he said, "I would welcome a patch that removed the GIL
"only if it does not hurt single-threaded code, "or it did not hurt multi-threaded code that was I/O bound."
That's a very high bar to reach.
I say that we also shouldn't break C extensions.
We broke every C extension out there with the introduction of Python 3.0, and it's taken us a long time for the C extensions to get ported up to it.
If we release a new version of Python and we say, "We removed the GIL.
"You're welcome. Oh, all of your C extensions broke. You're welcome," people are going to get annoyed with us. So let's not do that.
Let's not break the C extensions to the degree that we can preserve them.
And finally, don't make it too complicated.
And of course this is pretty fuzzy, but the idea here is that CPython is very easy to work on.
The code is very clear, it's very straightforward, it's very easy to modify, it's very easy to read and understand and reason about.
And if we complicate it by adding multi-core support, then that's going to hurt our ability to keep evolving
in the future, to modify it, fix bugs, maintain it, all those things.
So let's try to minimize the complexity that we introduce by getting rid of the GIL.
So, a quick detour: I want to talk about a couple of approaches I don't think will work.
People have said for years, "If only we could get rid "of reference counting and go to --" the correct term is "tracing garbage collection."
This is what everybody else does: Java, C# and the CLR, I think Rust, Go, D --
all the modern languages use garbage collection to reclaim objects, to manage object lifetime.
It's Python and just a couple others that use reference counting.
And conventional wisdom is that garbage collection -- tracing garbage collection is about as fast as reference counting.
So that's not going to hurt us.
Where it hurts us is, it's going to break all the C extensions.
This is a major change to the API. All the C extensions work.
It's also a more complicated API than reference counting.
Reference counting is actually a very simple API, very easy to get right.
And even there, we still have C extensions that are getting it wrong. It happens all the time.
If we introduce an even more complicated API that C extension authors have to use, we're going to make it harder to write C extensions,
we're going to make it harder for them to get correct, which is really going to add bugs, essentially.
So I would say, I don't think we can consider this for now.
Maybe it's something we can talk about in the future, but not now.
Software transactional memory: this is way cooler!
This is the coolest thing. Software transactional memory is amazing.
But it's also very early. So if you followed the work at all of Armin Rigo, he's been working on a branch of PyPy for a number of years
to add software transactional memory.
When he walks in the room, he's the smartest person in the room.
He's brilliant, and he's having trouble with it.
I think us mortals don't have a chance.
So, while performance would be amazing in software transactional memory and it would fix all sorts of problems,
it would obviously break every C extension out there to a crazy degree because it has an incredibly complicated and hard-to-get-right API.
I asked Armin, I was like, "Could we put the CPython on STM?" And he was like, "You don't want to do it. It's so hard to get right."
So I don't think that's approachable.
So instead, let's talk about what I proposed with the Gilectomy.
And I want to make it clear, by the way -- so, people say, "Oh you're removing the GIL?" I'm like, "No, I removed the GIL in April.
"Now I'm working on making it faster." So, all of these things have happened, and I have a Python interpreter that doesn't have a GIL
that can run some Python programs.
[laughter] Very few. So, reference counting: we keep reference counting.
Reference counting -- that's the API everybody expects, so it's not going to break any code.
And it is going to slow down. That's really the problem.
I'm using something called atomic incr and decr.
This is functionality you get free with every Intel processor.
This is the ability to add or subtract a number from any integer stored in your computer's RAM
in such a way that no other thread can fight you and have a race condition at the same time.
It guarantees that this increment or decrement will be atomic.
But it costs us a lot: it's 30% slower off the top.
I'm going to explore alternate approaches because this is hurting us a great deal with the Gilectomy.
Globals and static variables: it turns out this wasn't really a big deal.
First of all, the per-thread stuff had already, years ago, been moved into this PyThreadState variable.
I looked and I was like, "Oh, the work is done.
"I don't have to do anything here." These shared singletons: that's kind of the whole point of the Gilectomy.
Python, everything is public all the time. In order for Python to work, you have to be able to share stuff between threads.
So, yes, that just -- that's part of the package of the Gilectomy.
We don't have a problem here.
C extension parallelism and reentrancy, there's really no way around it.
It's -- we're going to break code and it's kind of the point to change the interpreter, and C extensions are going to break
when they first try to run under the Gilectomy.
And as far as the atomicity of operations, this is where we replace the one giant lock in Python
with millions, and I literally mean millions, of locks all over the place, little tiny locks.
So there's going to be a new lock API, at least internally.
That's what I've done in the Gilectomy.
I have macros called Py_LOCK and UNLOCK that you use kind of like Py_INCR and Py_DECR.
And then the PyTypeObject has sprouted an ob_lock method.
I don't know if it's exposed yet. I expect it to someday be exposed to functions and probably be called __lock__ and __unlock__.
Oh, sorry.
So what objects need to be locked?
Any mutable object. And when I say "mutable," I don't actually mean Python mutable, I mean C mutable.
So consider, for instance, the str object.
As Python programmers, you're like, "Oh, well, strs are immutable." And of course they are. But internally inside of CPython,
there are a bunch of lazily computed fields.
Like for instance, the hash value. We don't know the hash when we start up.
It's actually, we store a -1 as the hash value.
That's why -1 is an illegal value for hash.
So we store a -1 and we look and see, "Oh, it's -1 right now. We need to compute the hash."
If two threads came along and they both saw the -1, they would both compute the hash, and then both of them would overwrite it.
And in this case, it's not going to hurt anything. Like, two threads wasting a little time and overwriting each other's values
with the same computed value -- that's fine.
But there are two other fields, utf8 and wstr, that are internal representations of the string.
Those are computed lazily, and those both allocate memory.
And so if we had two threads that both computed those and overwrote, we're going to leak memory. That's bad.
So we would need some locking here. I don't know if we need a lock per string, or some global locks, or something.
but eventually, we're going to need to lock str objects.
I haven't done it right now so you can't use strs very much inside of the Gilectomy.
[laughter] Now, what kind of lock do you need?
You need what I'm going to call a userspace lock.
This is not technically -- like, people said, "Oh, userspace lock?
"That doesn't exist." What I mean here is, this is a lock that only uses userspace resources
like RAM until there is contention.
At the point that you have contention and you're talking about threads and scheduling, you need to involve the kernel.
And so you consume some kernel resources while there is contention.
Once the contention is gone, those resources should go away and you're back to only consuming RAM.
So, userspace locks are pretty common, actually.
Under Linux we have this onderful thing called the futex, which is a fast userspace lock. It's not actually a lock,
it's a lock primitive that you can use to make your own locking.
And I'm doing all my development under 64-bit Linux, so this is what I've been using.
Under Windows, there is a long-standing thing called the critical_section that I'm assured is userspace-only
until there's contention. And under OS X, I'm told that the standard pthread library from POSIX,
the pthread_mutex under OS X, is a userspace-only lock until there's contention. So I think we're already good
for a lot of the major platforms that we care about.
And the other platforms, I don't know what the answers are.
Again, it's very early days for the Gilectomy.
I'm assuming that they have similar answers here as well.
Now as far as these political constraints I talked about, I say that I can deliver a Gilectomy branch
that doesn't hurt single-threaded performance and doesn't break C extensions. Now you may remember,
mere slides ago I said we made it 30% slower off the top and every C extension breaks. So how can I claim this?
[laughter] The answer is: we have two builds.
You can build -- if we ever merge this -- and again, I don't know when it will happen -- we should be able to build Python
both with the GIL and without the GIL, and the "with-GIL" build would remain the default for probably a very long time.
So, "with the GIL" is what the Python we have today, and everything works exactly the same: your C extensions still work,
you still have the GIL, and your code doesn't break, which is great.
And then for the crazy futurists, we can compile it without the GIL, and that's when things like locking start happening.
So, we would have these -- these are all macros in C, which means that we can compile them away into nothing.
So Py_LOCK and Py_UNLOCK in the GIL build would do nothing.
And with the "without-GIL" build, they would now do something.
So, this means that we're complicating the CPython source code by having support for both "with the GIL" and "without the GIL"
on different lines, and you're going to have to read the code and understand in different contexts it means different things.
Now, in order to keep some sanity in the world, I propose that we also have two entry points on shared libraries.
So if you compile with the GIL, then you're going to have the same entry point you have today for a shared library, for a C extension.
And in the future you would have a different named entry point, which means that the "without-GIL" build is strictly opt-in.
This means that nobody's code breaks. You have to -- as an extension author, you have to say,
"I'm ready for no GIL. Here is the extension -- "here is the entry point that you can call "that means that you can load me in a no-GIL build."
This also has the nice feature of: you can examine a shared library externally and determine whether or not it supports no-GIL builds.
It might be possible in the future -- again, I haven't explored this yet -- but this is just sort of a note to myself.
If we took those macros and turned them into C functions and allowed you to call into them, we might be able to make it
so that you could write a single .so that supported both kinds of builds.
And it would just be like, oh, you call this one when you're in no-GIL and you call that one when you're with-GIL,
and you'd just have both of them in your code, kind of like we're going to have in CPython itself.
And that would let extension authors only compile once and not have to face as much complexity and just understand both.
But they wouldn't have to compile it twice and ship two different binaries.
Now, since effectively this is a new CAPI, it looks almost exactly like the existing CAPI, but we have this new locking stuff and some of the semantics are different.
Arguably this is kind of a different CAPI, and so this might be a good opportunity to say --
there are a bunch of things that are recommended practices in Python.
These are best practices for C extension authors, but they're not required. And it hurts us because
we have to support all this nasty old backwards compatibility behavior.
This might be a good opportunity to shed that and say, "You know what?
"Now, PyType_Ready -- that's no longer optional." This is something -- it's possible to create a type in Python
and introduce objects into the Python runtime without ever telling Python, "Hey, I have a new type for you."
This is what tells Python, "I have a new type for you." We might say, "Okay, it's required in no-GIL builds."
PEP 489 is this thing I don't quite understand, but it's a multiphase C extension initialization.
Again, it seems like it's a good idea. It might be a good time to say, "That's not optional anymore either."
Now remember when I said don't make it too complicated?
This is kind of where the Gilectomy is falling down a little bit.
Now we're going to have these two different builds, we're going to have code interleaved where this is with-GIL
and this is without-GIL. People have said, "We can live with this, Larry, if you can make it fast enough."
Now, I have been working on this for a couple of months.
My original codename was "Confuse-a-Cat." Then I thought of "Gilectomy" and I was like, "Oh, no, that's the name. We're done."
So, I've gone back a lot of times to this essay that Guido wrote in 2007 titled, "It isn't Easy to Remove the GIL"
on his old Artima blog. And I've reread it and reread it and I keep finding new things that he said.
It's really worth reading, and I agree with everything that he says, except the title, because it turns out, if you know where to start,
you can actually remove the GIL in about a week.
So, here is the list of all the things you need to do in order to remove the GIL.
Step 0: switch Py_INCR and Py_INCR to atomic incr and decr.
That's real easy. Step 2 -- step 1, I should say: decide on what locking mechanism you're going to use.
It has to be recursive.
It has to be userspace-only because you're going to have a lot of them.
Step 3: you have to add locking to the dictobject.
You go from top to bottom in the dictobject.c, everything that is an external entry point
for anybody calling into it from an exterior module, you have to add locking code. You have to lock at the top
and unlock at every exit.
Step 3: same thing for the list object.
You cannot run a Python interpreter without working dicts and lists, because CPython uses those internally
as part of the running mechanism of Python all over the place.
Step 4: there are ten freelists that are at global scope inside of CPython and you have to add locks around all of those.
Like, tuples, and I think integers, and PyFrame objects.
You just need to make sure that any time someone accesses that freelist, you have to lock and unlock.
Step 5: you have to totally disable the cyclic GC, the garbage collector.
And in particular, there are these track and untrack macros and you just have to stub those out, those have to be empty,
because they're -- those are called all the time.
Actually I originally had locking there and that was costing me 15% and causing crashes, and I just threw my hands in the air.
Step 6: finally it's time to remove the GIL.
You literally can just go and comment it out and you go and find the macros that are referring to it
and you just make them no-ops. You don't have a GIL anymore.
You can't run code quite yet, because step 7, you need to -- there's this PyThreadState that's storing the state
of the running interpreter, and you need to change it.
Right now in CPython, that's stored in a global variable, and it's just like, "That's the one. That's the thread state right now,"
and everyone refers to it. And whenever you switch threads, we overwrite that variable with the new thread state.
Instead, change it. It's already stored in thread-local storage, you just change the macros in the function so they return
the version that's in thread-local storage, and that works.
And finally there's just a couple of tests you need to fix.
Obviously all the multi-threaded tests aren't going to work.
Most of the multi -- most of the single-threaded tests actually still work. There are a couple of tests
that assert the size of dictobject and listobject, and we just change those by adding the lock to it.
So you just need to fix those so that the size is correct and then those tests will start running.
Yeah, people who are taking pictures, this is the final version of the slide.
I'm also uploading the slides so you can see this later.
Now, at the Language Summit I presented about this and I said, it's 3.5 times slower on wall time
and it's about 25 times slower on CPU time.
First, let me tell you, those numbers aren't correct.
Of course, I don't have correct numbers because the benchmarking is so terrible.
But let me explain what these numbers mean.
"Wall time" means: if you start the program and watch the wall -- the clock on the wall, that's how long it took.
So that's how long everything took to finish.
CPU time: my version is using multiple cores.
And so, if I'm using 6 cores at the same time, if it takes 3 seconds and I'm using 6 cores,
it's used 18 seconds of CPU time, right?
So, 25x, that's how much time we're actually spending -- that's the real CPU time. So, just to drive it home:
at 25x slower, that means that 4% of the time it's doing your work, and 96% of the time it's doing something else.
Now, just to show you what I've been doing, here is Gilectomy's official benchmark. It is a terrible Fibonacci function.
[laughter] Again, I can run very little code inside of the Gilectomy version of Python without it breaking. I can run integers,
I can run function calls, I can look things up in dicts, and in particular this is looking up fib in the module dict
over and over and over.
You can use strings if you're gentle.
There's a lot of stuff that I wouldn't try.
So, here are benchmarks that I ran on my computer the other night.
I actually ran these last night and on a computer that has 28 cores, so I'm not running out of cores. These are all hardware cores.
So, the number along the bottom is how many instances. It's fib 30.
So that's how many fib 30s I'm running on separate threads.
So I'm running threads in both CPython normal and the Gilectomy branch. The fast one is lower.
That's -- the y-axis is number of seconds.
The blue line is standard CPython, and the red line is the Gilectomy.
And I want to point out, first of all, the Gilectomy is way slower.
Second of all, there's this dip at four cores I don't understand.
It's just one of these things where probably everything meshed really well and I got lucky. It was consistent
so I couldn't get rid of it, so I'm just leaving it in the slides.
[laughter] I think the shape of the GIL -- the standard Python branch is linear and much faster,
and the shape of the Gilectomy version appears like, maybe it's sort of curving up?
I think it's probably going to keep going up. I don't know.
At one thread, you'll notice that the Gilectomy is actually not that much slower. It's only about twice as slow.
Which is great for me, but again, this is wall time, and I think CPU time is much more telling of the tale.
So, again, the Gilectomy version is about twice as slow at one thread.
At two threads, it jumps to 10x slower, and then it just keeps going up and up. Again, there's this anomaly at four.
when we get to 19 -- when we get to seven cores, it's a -- actually, I have a slide for this.
So, again, twice as slow on one core.
This is CPU time for the Gilectomy version divided by the CPU time for the GIL version.
So this is -- effectively the y-axis is now "how many x slower," and you can see at seven cores I am now 19x slower.
That hurts. Why is it so slow. Now, a lot of people, their first guess is, "Oh, that's going to be lock contention."
The answer is: there is a little bit of lock contention.
It's not actually that much.
The runtime of my program -- let me bring this back -- wall time -- CPU time, at seven cores I used, like, 90 seconds of CPU time, right?
So, lock contention, probably like five seconds of that.
It's measurable, it's noticeable, but it's not the major thing.
It's not costing us 96% of our time.
The major thing is really synchronization and cache misses.
What's going on here is that we're doing this atomic incr and decr.
Atomic incr and decr, in order to be safe, says, "You know what? Everyone's cache, you have to throw away this cache line
"for this object over here that's storing the reference count.
"Oh, and we just did it again because we changed the reference count.
"Oh, we just did it again because we changed the reference count." My test program on seven threads runs a half billion reference count changes.
And so we have effectively blown away the cache a half a billion times.
CPython didn't have to bother to do that, so it can do it in whatever it is, 6 seconds.
I'm blowing away the cache all the time so it takes me 90 seconds.
That's how important caching is on a modern computer.
The real problem here is that nothing is private inside of a Python interpreter.
So I'm doing the safe multi-threaded thing at every step in an attempt to make the Python code correct
and produce the correct result, and not crash.
But I have to do everything in the public, safe, multi-threaded way.
CPython, of course, doesn't have to bother. It's doing the fast, unsynchronized way because it's assured that only one thread is running at a time.
So that's really the challenge. Where we go from here: in general, I and the other people who are volunteering
to work on the Gilectomy, what we need to do is change the approach that we're doing.
So instead of doing the safe multi-threaded way, instead we modify the code so that we can guarantee
that we're only doing this work from a particular thread.
And then once we've guaranteed that, we can do it in the unsafe, unsynchronized way that is enormously faster, and we can reclaim that speed back.
So there are a bunch of techniques that I could talk about.
Under reference counting, the next thing I want to try is called buffered reference counting.
This is, very quickly, just the idea that instead of doing the reference count changes immediately,
instead you write them down and you send them off to a separate thread, and that thread is the guy who commits all the reference counts.
Since it's only one thread doing it, he can do it unsynchronized and he's fine.
We could try immortal objects.
Immortal objects would be a reference count that never changes, and you just look at that and you say,
"Oh, that's a reference count that never changes," and you don't change it. That means you don't have to change it,
which means you don't have any synchronization.
You get it for free, except for the 'if' statement.
Coalesced reference counting: that's where, instead of writing reference count changes right away, you just sort of keep a tally.
It's like, "Object O, I have added two references to it, so it's +2," and then I decrement it. Most of the time in C code,
